name: Laser for ingrown (pseudofolliculitis barbae)

lead: Pseudofolliculitis barbae (PFB) is a condition of inflamed bumps and ingrown hairs that occurs after shaving, mostly in people with tightly curled facial hair. Laser hair reduction, which thins the hair that causes the problem, is one treatment option described in dermatology literature.

Published clinical studies, including a long-pulsed 1064 nm Nd:YAG study in skin types IV to VI and a low-fluence 1064 nm trial, are small. Reference sources describe laser as a long-term option requiring at least six sessions.

paras: Shaving cuts curly hair at an angle, and the sharp tip can re-enter the skin and cause inflammation. Lasers target pigment in the hair follicle to reduce hair growth. Longer wavelengths such as 1064 nm are used for darker skin because they are less absorbed by skin pigment.

Reported effects include redness and pigment changes. Skin type, device and settings influence risk. Other options described in the literature include allowing hair to grow, chemical peels, topical agents and eflornithine.

lead: Pseudofolliculitis barbae (PFB), commonly 'razor bumps' or 'ingrowns', is an inflammatory condition in which shaved, curved hairs re-enter the skin and cause papules, pustules and sometimes pigmentation or scarring [1][2]. It is most common in men with tightly curled beard hair and is associated with a keratin gene variant (K6hf A12T) [3][2].

Laser hair reduction is among the treatments described for PFB. Reference sources call permanent follicle removal the definitive treatment [4], while studies of laser use in darker skin types focus on long-pulsed Nd:YAG at 1064 nm [5][6]. Looksmaxxing discussion of the procedure sits alongside clean-shaven grooming and skin-quality goals.
infobox: At least six, 4 to 6 weeks apart (reference sources)
Growing the beard, peels, topical agents, eflornithine, electrolysis

paras: PFB results from hair being cut short and curling back, with transfollicular or extrafollicular penetration leading to a foreign-body inflammatory reaction [1][2]. A genetic variant in the companion-layer keratin K6hf has been identified as a risk factor [3], and general work on hair keratins and their disorders supports a role for follicle structure [7][8]. Reference sources state that curly hair and shaving technique are the main risk factors [4].

A 2002 study treated PFB in skin types IV, V and VI with a long-pulsed Nd:YAG laser [5], and a review covers laser-assisted hair removal for darker skin [6]. Pulsed alexandrite, diode and Nd:YAG lasers are used, with Nd:YAG preferred for darker pigmentation, and at least six sessions spaced 4 to 6 weeks apart are typical [4]. Side effects include redness and discolouration [4].
A tertiary laser unit's experience also describes PFB as one of the less common indications of laser hair removal [9].

The literature describes allowing the beard to grow for several weeks, glycolic and salicylic acid peels, benzoyl peroxide, topical or oral antibiotics and retinoids [10][11][4]. Registered trials have tested eflornithine cream [12][13], a pre-shave gel and brush [14], and a powder depilatory (withdrawn) [15].

A long-pulsed Nd:YAG study in skin types IV to VI is published [5]. A registered trial of low-fluence 1064 nm laser hair reduction for PFB enrolled 22 participants (completed) [16]. Registered non-laser trials include eflornithine cream (n=15, completed [13]; n=9, terminated [12]) and a pre-shave gel and brush (n=29) [14]. Trials are small and no large randomised laser trials are listed.
